slides.title: Clock proteins create a delayed negative-feedback cycle
body: The mammalian molecular clock contains a **delayed negative-feedback loop**. Proteins including CLOCK and BMAL1 promote transcription of genes such as Period and Cryptochrome. Transcription produces RNA, which is then translated into PER and CRY proteins. These steps introduce time between activation of the genes and accumulation of their protein products.

As PER and CRY accumulate and enter the nucleus, they suppress the transcriptional activity that helped produce them. Their own production consequently declines. Later, modification and degradation remove enough inhibitory protein for transcription to rise again, beginning another cycle of synthesis, accumulation, inhibition, and removal within the cell.

The delay is essential to the rhythm. Immediate feedback would tend to hold the system near a steady level, whereas time-consuming production, transport, and degradation allow it to cycle. Changes in protein stability can lengthen or shorten the interval, connecting a molecular alteration to the period observed in an animal's daily behavior.

slides.title: Individual clock cells normally keep coordinated rhythms
body: Hayasaka and colleagues studied the clock protein PER2 using a **luciferase reporter**. Luciferase produces light through a chemical reaction, allowing changes in a linked clock signal to be followed over time. Cultured SCN slices continued producing rhythmic light signals after removal from the animal, demonstrating that the preparation retained an internal timing process.

The source recording shows a normal mouse SCN slice across successive cycles. Individual cells change their light output, and their timing is coordinated enough to produce an organized population rhythm. The changing brightness reports the molecular reporter rather than ordinary neural electrical spikes or a flash of calcium associated with a single action potential.

The investigators measured both **period**, the time between cycles, and **phase**, the position of a cell within its cycle. Two cells can have similar periods while reaching their peaks at different times. Following single cells therefore reveals whether a weak population rhythm arises from weak individual oscillators or from oscillators whose peaks no longer align.

slides.title: Light can advance or delay a circadian clock
body: A **phase advance** moves a rhythm earlier, while a **phase delay** moves it later. In many circumstances, light late in the biological night advances the human clock, whereas light earlier in the biological night delays it. These effects depend on internal phase, so civil clock time alone cannot specify the response for every person.

Repeated light exposures can entrain a clock whose natural period differs slightly from the environmental day. Small daily adjustments compensate for that difference, keeping sleep-related and hormonal rhythms near a stable relationship to sunrise and sunset. A brief light-induced change in alertness is separate from this lasting adjustment of the clock's phase.

A **phase-response curve** plots the direction and size of resetting against the biological time of the stimulus. Its advance and delay regions explain why identical evening and morning exposures can shift timing in opposite directions. When the external schedule changes, the clock must undergo a sequence of these adjustments before its outputs realign.

slides.title: SIK3 loss destabilizes molecular clock coordination
body: **SIK3** is an enzyme that contributes to regulation of clock-protein stability. Hayasaka and colleagues compared SCN slices from normal mice with slices lacking SIK3. The mutant cells displayed a broader distribution of periods and phases, producing less coordinated molecular rhythms across the tissue despite the continued presence of many oscillating cells.

The source movie follows the SIK3-deficient preparation using the same PER2-linked light reporter as the normal slice. A population image can lose a coherent rhythm when individual cells peak at different times. Single-cell tracking showed that the altered signal involved instability and desynchronization rather than simply disappearance of all cellular clock activity.

Additional experiments found increased PER2 abundance when SIK3 was reduced and lower PER2 abundance when SIK3 was increased. The effect involved phosphorylation-dependent destabilization of PER2, directly or through intermediate steps. Slowing removal of an inhibitory clock protein changes feedback timing, providing a molecular route to the altered daily rhythms observed in the animals.

slides.title: Dawn and dusk reshape molecular clock waveforms
body: Kim and McMahon simulated light input directly in cultured SCN tissue using an optogenetic channel. They monitored PER2-linked bioluminescence before and after stimulation at different circadian phases. Because the preparation was outside the animal, the experiment could examine clock resetting without requiring a change in locomotion, feeding, or the timing of sleep.

Stimulation altered the shape of the molecular waveform as well as its peak time. Rising and falling phases changed in duration, producing an asymmetric cycle during resetting. Advancing or delaying the clock therefore involved changing the progression of the molecular process, rather than moving an otherwise unchanged curve along the time axis.

Different SCN regions showed different responses. Acute waveform shifts were strongest in the ventrolateral region, while period effects were greater dorsomedially. Repeated stimulation resembling different seasonal day lengths also reshaped the rhythms, providing a cellular mechanism through which the clock network can represent both daily timing and the duration of environmental light.

slides.title: A living SCN contains fast and slow calcium rhythms
body: El Cheikh Hussein and colleagues recorded calcium in SCN neurons of freely behaving mice using a miniature imaging system. Each signal contained fast calcium events superimposed on a more slowly changing baseline. Measuring those components separately allowed the investigators to compare rapid cellular activity with changes distributed across the daily cycle.

The source movie shows an acquired SCN recording at the authors' accelerated playback speed. Individual brightening events occur within a tissue field whose overall fluorescence also changes more slowly. The fast event rate and the baseline are different features of the same measurement, so averaging them together would remove information about how each neuron operates.

Daily changes in baseline calcium were relatively coordinated across neurons, while the times of peak fast-event activity were more diverse. A cell could therefore share the population's broad daily organization while producing its rapid events at a different time. The living clock combined temporal unity at one scale with diversity at another.

slides.title: Melatonin communicates the timing of darkness
body: **Melatonin** is a hormone released by the pineal gland, with secretion normally increasing during the biological night. It communicates information about darkness and circadian phase to tissues containing melatonin receptors. Its rise is a useful timing signal, but it is not an electrical command that forces every brain region into sleep.

The SCN influences the pineal gland through a pathway involving the hypothalamus, spinal cord, and sympathetic neurons in the superior cervical ganglion. Norepinephrine released at the pineal gland promotes the biochemical steps needed for nighttime melatonin synthesis. The route therefore converts clock-network output into a circulating hormonal signal through several identifiable neural stages.

Light at night can suppress melatonin secretion through retinal input to this system. Researchers often measure **dim-light melatonin onset**, the evening rise recorded under controlled low illumination, to estimate internal circadian phase. Keeping light low during measurement reduces immediate light suppression that could otherwise obscure when the hormone's nightly rise would occur.

slides.title: Protein phosphorylation changes the lifetime of PER2
body: A **kinase** is an enzyme that adds phosphate groups to proteins. Philpott and colleagues studied casein kinase 1, which phosphorylates the clock protein PER2 at different sites. Modification at one group of sites can stabilize PER2, while modification at another can favor its recognition by the machinery that removes proteins from the cell.

The kinase's three-dimensional shape influences which sites it modifies efficiently. The source animation represents the authors' computed modes of motion, including opening and twisting of parts of the enzyme. It is a molecular model derived from structural analysis, rather than a microscope recording of one enzyme moving inside a sleeping brain.

Mutations that changed the kinase's structural behavior also shifted its relative action on stabilizing and degradation-related sites. This **phosphoswitch** alters how long PER2 remains available to inhibit the clock's transcriptional machinery. Changing the lifetime of that inhibitory protein changes the delay in the feedback cycle and can consequently change the circadian period.

slides.title: Evening caffeine can delay the human melatonin rhythm
body: Burke and colleagues tested whether evening caffeine changes circadian timing in addition to increasing alertness. Participants received caffeine or a placebo before their habitual bedtime under controlled laboratory conditions. The researchers measured the melatonin rhythm before and after treatment, separating a shift in internal timing from the person's immediate feeling of being more awake.

Caffeine taken three hours before habitual bedtime delayed the subsequent melatonin rhythm by about forty minutes under the tested conditions. An evening bright-light condition also delayed the rhythm. These comparisons show why an intervention's timing is part of its biological action: the same exposure can affect tonight's alertness and the placement of the internal night.

In cultured human cells carrying clock reporters, caffeine lengthened molecular rhythms through mechanisms involving adenosine-receptor signaling and cyclic AMP, an intracellular messenger. A cell-level effect did not require a person to stay awake later by choice. The experiments therefore identified both a human phase shift and a plausible receiving-cell pathway through which caffeine can alter clock function.

slides.title: Morning sleep loss produces strong rebound in flies
body: Andreani and colleagues deprived flies of sleep for the same short duration at different times of day. After deprivation ending in the morning, the animals showed strong recovery sleep. The original recording follows the hours after that morning interruption, with source time labels showing how the accelerated movie corresponds to the behavioral observation period.

The researchers measured rebound relative to baseline sleep at the same time of day. This comparison matters because an animal may normally sleep more in the morning than in the evening. Additional sleep after deprivation must be separated from the daily sleep pattern that would have occurred even without the experimental interruption.

Neurons in the **ellipsoid body**, a central fly-brain structure, participate in tracking sleep need. After morning sleep loss, a defined group showed increased calcium and changes in presynaptic markers. The clock could therefore influence the cellular response to recent waking, rather than contributing only a separate signal added to an otherwise time-independent homeostat.

slides.title: Jet lag and shift work misalign internal and external time
body: **Jet lag** occurs when the internal clock remains aligned with the previous time zone while the environment has changed. Local bedtime can then arrive during the traveler's biological day, or waking obligations can occur during the internal night. Sleepiness, appetite, and temperature rhythms may initially occur at inconvenient local times.

Different body systems need not reset at the same rate. Light can change SCN timing, while meal timing influences clocks in metabolic tissues. During adjustment, central and peripheral rhythms may temporarily adopt different relationships, so returning to a regular bedtime does not instantly realign every physiological cycle.

Night-shift work can create recurring misalignment when a person must be active during the biological night and sleep during daylight. Daytime light, social schedules, and days off can oppose adaptation to the shift. The resulting sleep pattern depends on both accumulated pressure and the clock's continued promotion of alertness during part of the intended sleep period.

slides.title: The same sleep loss produces less rebound in the evening
body: When the same duration of deprivation ended in the evening, Andreani and colleagues observed less rebound than after morning deprivation. The source movie shows the greater activity during the later recovery interval. Equal time kept awake therefore did not produce equal immediate recovery sleep at every circadian phase.

The ellipsoid-body neurons also responded differently: the calcium increase observed after morning sleep loss was not present in the same way after evening loss. Clock-neuron manipulations changed this time-dependent regulation. The homeostatic circuit's cellular response was therefore being programmed by circadian input, rather than responding only to the number of minutes awake.

The investigators distinguished clock populations associated with morning and evening timing. Their influence on rebound could be separated from effects on the ordinary daily locomotor rhythm. A clock circuit can regulate how sleep need is expressed without producing an identical change in every behavior that normally varies across the day.

slides.title: Light changes activity across the human hypothalamus
body: Light can influence alertness and cognition in addition to resetting circadian phase. Campbell and colleagues used high-field functional MRI while participants performed auditory tasks under different illumination levels. The measurement detects blood-oxygenation-related changes, allowing small hypothalamic regions to be compared while visual illumination changes during an ongoing cognitive task.

Brighter illumination increased the measured response in posterior hypothalamic regions while decreasing it in some anterior and ventral regions. The hypothalamus therefore did not respond as one uniform block. Areas containing parts of arousal-related and clock-related systems showed different response patterns within the same broad anatomical structure.

Executive-task performance also improved under brighter conditions, but an anatomical MRI region contains several cell types and small nuclei. Its blood-related signal cannot identify the firing of a specific orexin or histamine neuron. The experiment measures a regional human response to light, complementing cellular studies that can isolate particular receiving neurons and receptors.

slides.title: Conflicting time cues can disrupt an animal's rhythms
body: A **zeitgeber** is an environmental timing cue that can synchronize a biological rhythm. Berger and Tarrant studied light and temperature cues in the sea anemone Nematostella. Temperature cycles organized daily locomotor behavior, allowing the investigators to test what happens when more than one environmental signal supplies information about time.

The source recording follows real anemone movement with a computer-tracked center point. The authors accelerated playback, so the visible motion spans a much longer behavioral interval than its screen duration. Tracking converts changes in position into a time series that can be compared with the light and temperature schedules experienced by the animal.

When the light and temperature cycles were chronically misaligned, behavioral and gene-expression rhythms became disrupted. Some metabolic genes nevertheless retained rhythms related to temperature. Conflicting cues therefore affected parts of the rhythmic system differently, rather than requiring every measured process to lose its daily organization at the same moment.

slides.title: Brain and body clocks coordinate different daily functions
body: Many tissues contain cellular clocks, including the liver, pancreas, and other organs involved in metabolism. Their rhythms can organize when enzymes, transporters, and hormone responses are most active. The SCN coordinates these systems through neural and hormonal outputs while the tissues also respond to local signals such as the timing of food intake.

Coordination does not require every organ to peak at the same hour. A useful relationship may place one process before another, such as preparing metabolic pathways before a predictable feeding period. **Internal synchrony** means maintaining appropriate phase relationships among rhythms, not making every physiological measurement rise and fall together.

A change in external schedule can temporarily alter those relationships. The light-sensitive central clock, feeding-sensitive peripheral tissues, and sleep-pressure system receive different information and operate through different mechanisms. Recording several outputs, such as melatonin, activity, meals, and temperature, reveals which parts have shifted and which remain aligned with the earlier schedule.

slides.title: Sleep cycles can repeat within the daily rhythm
body: An **ultradian rhythm** repeats more often than once per day. Medeiros and colleagues observed recurring active-sleep episodes in octopuses, commonly separated by longer quiet-sleep periods. Many intervals between active episodes were roughly half an hour, providing a shorter cycle nested within the animal's broader daily pattern of behavior.

The source recording shows active sleep at night, with changing skin patterns and small movements. Comparing this bout with daytime examples establishes that the visible state can occur in more than one part of the daily cycle. Its classification depends on the combined state features, rather than the time of day alone.

Circadian timing and ultradian state transitions therefore describe different levels of organization. A daily rhythm can influence when sleep is likely, while the sleeping animal alternates between shorter recurring states. Counting active episodes without their quiet-sleep intervals would miss the sequence that gives those bouts their place within the overall sleep pattern.

slides.title: Measure sleep pressure and clock timing separately
body: Sleep can be measured along several independent dimensions: when it occurs, how long it lasts, how its stages are arranged, and how strongly the animal responds to stimulation. Electrical intensity adds another dimension. A manipulation that increases slow-wave activity has changed a different quantity from one that merely lengthens the opportunity to remain asleep.

Homeostatic experiments alter recent sleep history, while circadian experiments measure or manipulate biological time. Comparing deprivation at several phases can reveal interactions between these systems. Measuring melatonin or another clock marker helps determine whether a delayed sleep period reflects changed internal timing, accumulated waking, or a combination of both influences.

After prolonged waking, stronger early-night slow-wave activity can indicate elevated sleep pressure. If melatonin onset also occurs later, the clock has shifted as well. A longer sleep period alone cannot distinguish these changes: the electrical intensity and phase marker provide separate measurements needed to identify the contributions of recent waking and internal biological time.

items.lead: Sleep is an active, reversible state.
items.text: Combine behavior, responsiveness, and electrical or physiological measurements to identify its organization.
Recent waking changes homeostatic need, while circadian circuits regulate when that need is expressed.
Inhibitory sleep circuits, arousal transmitters, orexin, and glial signaling change distinct properties of sleep.
Slow oscillations, spindles, and hippocampal ripples coordinate activity relevant to memory processing.
Narcolepsy, cataplexy, parasomnias, and apnea disrupt different combinations of awareness, muscle control, and physiology.
Light resets SCN networks, while protein turnover and tissue coordination determine daily phase and period.
